sentences.text: Rhamphosuchus was an extinct genus of gavialoid crocodilians found in the Indian subcontinent, characterized by large bodies and elongated, narrow jaws typical of the group.

Unlike modern gharials, these species were more robust with snouts that widened toward the head and closely spaced teeth forming an alligator-like overbite, while the lower jaw tip remained less expanded than in derived gavialoids.
Each premaxilla contained five teeth, matching the count in modern Indian gharials, and deep pits on the upper jaw may have served as insertion points for a sensory structure.
R. crassidens could reach body lengths of 8 to 11 meters based on rigorous estimates of known specimens, though this means it is not the largest known crocodilian.
While early researcher Richard Lydekker estimated R. crassidens reached 15 to 18 meters, a 2025 estimate suggests R. pachyrhynchus reached body lengths of 6 to 8 meters.
Analysis of R. pachyrhynchus shows its teeth became much more tightly packed together than in modern gavialoids as the animal aged.
The genus Rhamphosuchus was originally described by Falconer and Cautley in 1840, later re-described by Richard Lydekker in 1886.
The holotype, defined as the specimen the species is based on, is a partial snout tip catalogued as NHMUK PV OR 39802.
Gudrun Corvinus and H. Hermann Schleich described a snout tip from Rato Khola and isolated teeth from Surai Khola as part of the Surai Khola Formation.
Gavialis leptodus was once speculated to represent a juvenile Rhamphosuchus.

Researchers suggest Rhamphosuchus had a generalist diet due to its robust build and large size, unlike the mostly fish-eating gharial, and probably had a more generalized carnivorous diet than the ichthyophagy of other tomistomine crocodilians.

It is possible that Rhamphosuchus preyed on chalicotheres, rhinos, and possibly juvenile Paraceratherium, as fossil bones of large Oligocene mammals like chalicotheres and Paraceratherium in the Bugti Hills show tooth marks from giant crocodilians.

Fossils of chalicotheres and rhinos found in the same formations as Rhamphosuchus bear bitemarks from a large crocodilian, and it is possible that Rhamphosuchus attacked other crocodilians, supported by bite marks found on Miocene Gavialis fossils.

Warm temperatures, extensive wetlands, and high ecosystem productivity likely allowed Rhamphosuchus to grow to its large size, and Walter and colleagues hypothesize that gigantism in crocodyliforms like Rhamphosuchus was driven by extensive marine or wetland biomes.
Analysis of Rhamphosuchus pachyrhynchus shows its snout width increased much more rapidly than other skull dimensions during growth.

Scientists debate whether Rhamphosuchus is a relative of the modern false gharial (Tomistominae) or the Indian gharial (Gavialoidea), and the precise phylogenetic position of Rhamphosuchus within Gavialoidea remains uncertain among researchers.
Rhamphosuchus crassidens lacks the expanded snout tip found in R. pachyrhynchus.
Fossils of Rhamphosuchus date to the Possibly Early Middle Pleistocene.
The older species R. pachyrhynchus is known from Oligocene and Miocene deposits in Pakistan's Bugti and Laki Hills and possibly the Khari Nadi Formation of Kutch.

Rhamphosuchus crassidens may have lived during the Late Pliocene and Early Middle Pleistocene based on associated fauna like Camelus sivalensis and Ursus sivalensis, while fossils referred to R. crassidens from Nepal are roughly Middle Pliocene in age and found in strata correlated to the Tatrot/Pinjor faunal zone of India and the Upper Siwaliks in Pakistan.
It is debated whether the bitemarks on rhino fossils belong to Rhamphosuchus, as other large crocodilians shared the same environment.

Jason J. Head suggests the hypodigm of Rhamphosuchus could be chimeric, with some specimens belonging to a different animal, and Courville and colleagues are hesitant to assign certain Nepalese remains to Rhamphosuchus crassidens, referring them instead to cf. Rhamphosuchus sp. due to tooth spacing.
